title: Blood glucose and specimen collection
blurb: Measure capillary glucose accurately, treat hypoglycaemia step by step, and collect and interpret urine, stool, sputum and vomit specimens.
question: Mrs Achterberg, 71, takes gliclazide. Before lunch she is sweaty and shaky but alert and able to swallow. Her capillary glucose is 3.2 mmol/L. What is the correct first treatment and when should it be rechecked?

teach.body: Capillary blood glucose, urinalysis and specimens of urine, stool, sputum and vomit are routine investigations a registered nurse collects, observes, interprets, records and acts on. Formally they are point-of-care tests and microbiological samples. In plain English: a good sample, taken the right way at the right time, gives the team the information to treat the person correctly; a poor one wastes time or misleads.

items: Ask the person to wash their hands with soap and warm water and dry them thoroughly: sugar on the skin, for example from fruit, can give a falsely high reading.
Do not use wet wipes, which can contain substances that affect the result.
Warm hands bleed more easily. Prick the side of the fingertip, avoiding the thumb and index finger, and rotate fingers.
Apply the drop to the strip, record the result with the time, and act on it.
In a very sick or peri-arrest person, finger-prick results can be unreliable: use a venous or arterial sample (RCUK).

teach.h: Capillary glucose in an adult with diabetes in hospital

bands.label: 'Looming' hypo: act if on insulin or SU

teach.caption: JBDS 2023: treat any glucose below 4.0 mmol/L, with or without symptoms. If symptomatic above 4.0, give a carbohydrate snack.

teach.h: Conscious, cooperative and able to swallow (JBDS algorithm A)

steps.label: Still under 4.0?
steps.sub: After 30–45 min or 3 cycles: call medical help

steps.label: Above 4.0
steps.sub: Give 20 g long-acting carbohydrate, e.g. two biscuits

steps.label: Prevent recurrence
steps.sub: Do not omit insulin if due; review regimen; document

teach.caption: If an insulin infusion is running, stop it immediately and restart once the hypo is treated. Pure fruit juice (150–200 mL) is not suitable on a low-potassium diet.

teach.h: Treatment depends on what the person can safely do

rows.label: Alternative
values: IV glucose or glucagon 1 mg IM

teach.caption: IV options (JBDS): 100 mL of 20% or 200 mL of 10% glucose over 15 minutes. Glucagon is less effective with sulfonylureas, alcohol excess, liver disease or malnutrition.

teach.body: Send a midstream urine (MSU) for culture before antibiotics, filling boric acid containers to the line, and never dipstick from a boric acid container. For a catheter, take the specimen from the sampling port, not the bag. Sputum should be coughed up from deep in the chest, not saliva, ideally before antibiotics (NICE NG15). For stool and vomit, record amount, colour, consistency and contents; use soap and water for hand hygiene with diarrhoea.
teach.cite: UKHSA UTI diagnostic tools; NICE NG15; NIPCM

teach.caption: Dipsticks rule infection in but are unreliable for ruling it out. A morning sample is more reliable for nitrites, as bacteria need 4 hours or more to produce them.
Type 1 has spent the longest time in the bowel, type 7 the least. Types 3 and 4 are normal (Bladder and Bowel UK).

teach.h: Worked example: Mrs Achterberg's hypo on a medical ward
items: 11:30: sweaty, shaky, alert, swallowing safely; capillary glucose 3.2 mmol/L. She chooses glucose tablets: 5–7 tablets (15–20 g).
11:45: rechecked at 15 minutes: 3.6 mmol/L, still under 4.0. A second 15–20 g dose is given.
11:58: 4.8 mmol/L and she feels better. She eats two biscuits (20 g long-acting carbohydrate), as lunch is not due for another hour.
The nurse documents the event, informs the doctor so her gliclazide can be reviewed, and plans regular glucose monitoring.

teach.text: Two traps. 'Four is the floor': 4.0 mmol/L, not 3.0 or 3.5, is the treatment threshold. And after a hypo, do not simply omit the next insulin dose: JBDS says do not omit insulin if due, but review the regimen.

items: Wash and dry hands before a capillary glucose; side of the fingertip.
Hypoglycaemia is under 4.0 mmol/L: 15–20 g fast carbohydrate, recheck in 10–15 minutes, up to 3 cycles, then medical help.
Confused but swallowing: glucose gel; unconscious: nothing by mouth, IV glucose or IM glucagon.
No urine dipsticks for over-65s or catheterised adults; MSU or sampling port specimen before antibiotics.
Bristol Stool Chart: types 3–4 normal, 1–2 constipation, 6–7 diarrhoea.

summary: You can now take an accurate capillary glucose, treat hypoglycaemia according to the JBDS algorithms, and know when a dipstick helps and when it misleads. You can collect urine, sputum, stool and vomit specimens correctly and describe stool using the Bristol Stool Chart.

A.q: Below what capillary glucose should an adult with diabetes in hospital be treated for hypoglycaemia, whether or not they have symptoms?
options: Below 3.0 mmol/L
Below 3.5 mmol/L
Below 5.0 mmol/L
Below 4.0 mmol/L
A.why: JBDS 2023: all non-pregnant adults with diabetes in hospital with a glucose below 4.0 mmol/L should be treated: '4.0 is the floor'.

whyNot.0: 3.0 mmol/L is too low a threshold; treatment starts below 4.0.
whyNot.1: 3.5 mmol/L is not the JBDS threshold; it is below 4.0.
whyNot.2: Levels of 4.0–6.0 are a 'looming' hypo warranting attention, but the treatment threshold is below 4.0.

A.q: Mr Daniels is conscious and can swallow. His glucose is 3.4 mmol/L. How much rapid-acting carbohydrate should be given first?
A.why: JBDS: 15–20 g of rapid-acting carbohydrate is the treatment of choice for a conscious person who can swallow, for example 5–7 glucose tablets.

whyNot.0: 5–10 g is too little to reliably correct hypoglycaemia.
whyNot.2: 40 g is the long-acting snack size after glucagon, not the first fast-acting dose.
whyNot.3: 25–30 g is more than the recommended first dose and may cause rebound hyperglycaemia.

A.q: A healthcare assistant describes Mr Lowe's stool as 'fluffy pieces with ragged edges, a mushy stool'. Which Bristol Stool Chart type is this?
options: Type 6
Type 4
Type 5
Type 7
A.why: Bristol type 6 is fluffy pieces with ragged edges, a mushy stool.

whyNot.1: Type 4 is a smooth, soft sausage or snake: normal.
whyNot.2: Type 5 is soft blobs with clear-cut edges.
whyNot.3: Type 7 is watery with no solid pieces, entirely liquid.

B.q: After giving oral glucose for hypoglycaemia, when should the nurse recheck the capillary glucose?
options: After 30 minutes
After 60 minutes
After 10–15 minutes
At the next meal
B.why: JBDS: repeat the capillary glucose 10–15 minutes after oral treatment; if still under 4.0 mmol/L, repeat the treatment.

whyNot.0: 30 minutes delays the second treatment if the first has not worked.
whyNot.1: An hour is far too long to leave a possible ongoing hypo unchecked.
whyNot.3: Waiting for a meal risks further, more severe hypoglycaemia.

B.q: Mr Kemp, 78, has new dysuria and urgency. A healthcare assistant offers to dipstick his urine. Under UKHSA guidance, what is the best response?
options: Dipstick it and treat if nitrites are positive
Do not dipstick; send urine for culture
Dipstick it and treat if leucocytes are present
Do not test, as symptoms alone confirm it
B.why: UKHSA: do not perform urine dipsticks in adults over 65, because asymptomatic bacteriuria is common and gives positive results without infection. Send urine for culture before antibiotics when UTI is suspected.

whyNot.0: Positive nitrites in an older adult may reflect harmless bacteriuria, so a dipstick misleads here.
whyNot.2: Leucocytes are common in older adults without infection; the dipstick is not used over 65.
whyNot.3: A urine culture is still needed to confirm the infection and guide antibiotics.

B.q: Mrs Pryce, 66, takes insulin. Her glucose is 2.9 mmol/L; she is confused and uncooperative but can swallow. Which treatment does JBDS guidance describe?
options: 150 mL of fruit juice offered with a straw
1 mg of glucagon given intravenously
A meal once she has calmed down
Two tubes of 40% glucose gel into the mouth
B.why: JBDS algorithm B: if the person is not capable or cooperative but can swallow, squeeze 2 tubes of 40% glucose gel between the teeth and gums, or give glucagon 1 mg IM if this is ineffective.

whyNot.0: Juice relies on cooperation she cannot currently give.
whyNot.1: Glucagon is given intramuscularly in this algorithm, not intravenously.
whyNot.2: Waiting for her to calm down delays treatment of a hypo that is causing the confusion.

C.q: Mr Okoye, 59, has been treated three times with 15–20 g of glucose tablets over 40 minutes. His glucose is now 3.1 mmol/L. He is alert and can swallow. What should the nurse do next?
options: Call medical help; consider IV glucose or glucagon
Give a fourth dose of glucose tablets and recheck
Give a 20 g long-acting snack and recheck later
Recheck his glucose in 1 hour before acting
C.why: JBDS: if the glucose remains under 4.0 mmol/L after 30–45 minutes or 3 treatment cycles, call for medical assistance; glucagon 1 mg IM or IV glucose may be considered.

whyNot.1: JBDS limits oral treatment to 3 cycles before medical help is called.
whyNot.2: The long-acting snack is given once the glucose is above 4.0, not while still hypoglycaemic.
whyNot.3: Waiting an hour leaves him hypoglycaemic when escalation is due now.

C.q: After treatment for a hypo, Mr Reid's glucose is 5.2 mmol/L and he feels well. His usual insulin is due with his evening meal in 20 minutes. What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Omit his next insulin dose to avoid a repeat
Give a second glucose drink and hold food
Hold all food until the doctor reviews him
Give a starchy snack and do not omit his insulin
C.why: JBDS: once above 4.0 mmol/L give a long-acting carbohydrate (or the next meal if due), and do not omit an insulin injection that is due, although the regimen should be reviewed.

whyNot.0: JBDS specifically says do not omit insulin if due; omission risks hyperglycaemia and ketoacidosis in insulin-dependent people.
whyNot.1: A further fast-acting drink is not needed above 4.0, and holding food risks a recurrence.
whyNot.2: Withholding food after a hypo risks another hypo.

C.q: Mrs Lam, 80, has a long-term urinary catheter and suspected catheter-associated UTI. What is the correct way to obtain a urine specimen?
options: Dipstick urine from the drainage bag
Collect urine from the bag for culture
Disconnect the catheter from the bag to collect
Take it from the sampling port before antibiotics
C.why: UKHSA: do not dipstick in catheterised adults; send a specimen from the sample port (or from a new catheter if it is changed) for culture before antibiotics, labelled with catheter details.

whyNot.0: Dipsticks are not used with catheters because bacteria are almost always present without infection.
whyNot.1: Urine in the bag has stood and is contaminated, so it gives misleading culture results.
whyNot.2: Breaking the closed drainage system increases the risk of infection.

reteach.title: Rule of 15 and the four-is-the-floor habit
reteach.question: Picture a clock and a sugar lump. What do you give, and when do you look again?

blocks.body: For a conscious person who can swallow: give 15–20 g of fast sugar, wait 10–15 minutes, recheck. Still under 4.0? Repeat, up to three times. Still low after that, or after 30–45 minutes, call medical help. Once above 4.0, give a slower carbohydrate so it does not drop again, and do not skip the next insulin.

blocks.text: Older adults and catheterised adults: no urine dipstick. A positive result often reflects harmless bacteria, not infection.

explain.body: Wash hands with soap and warm water and dry thoroughly; no wet wipes. Prick the side of the fingertip, avoiding thumb and index finger. Use a venous sample if the person is peri-arrest.

test.q: Mrs Dean has just peeled an orange and asks for her glucose to be checked. What should happen first?
options: Clean her finger with a wet wipe
Wipe off the first drop with gauze
Wash her hands with soap and water
Use her thumb, as it bleeds easily
test.why: Sugar on the skin can falsely raise the reading, so hands are washed with soap and warm water and dried thoroughly; wet wipes can contain substances that affect the result.

whyNot.0: Wet wipes may contain chemicals that affect the result and are not recommended.
whyNot.1: Wiping a drop does not remove fruit sugar from the skin as reliably as washing.
whyNot.3: The thumb and index finger are avoided; use the side of another fingertip.

explain.body: Options for 15–20 g: 5–7 glucose tablets, 60 mL glucose juice shot, 150–200 mL pure fruit juice, or 3–4 heaped teaspoons of sugar in water. Fruit juice is unsuitable on a low-potassium diet; sugar in water does not work with acarbose.

test.q: Which person should NOT be given fruit juice to treat hypoglycaemia?
options: Someone on a low-potassium diet
Someone with type 2 diabetes
Someone who is fasting tomorrow
Someone who takes metformin
test.why: JBDS: do not use pure fruit juice for people on a low-potassium diet, for example for chronic kidney disease, because of its potassium content.

whyNot.1: Fruit juice is a suitable choice in type 2 diabetes.
whyNot.2: Fasting the next day does not stop juice being used to treat a hypo now.
whyNot.3: Metformin is not a reason to avoid fruit juice.

explain.body: MSU for culture before antibiotics. Fill boric acid containers to the line; do not dipstick from them. No dipsticks over 65 or with a catheter; catheter specimens come from the sampling port.

test.q: A midstream urine is collected into a container with boric acid preservative. Which statement is correct?
options: Dipstick the urine in it before sending
Fill it to the marked line before sending
Add tap water if the volume is low
Leave the lid loose to let gas escape
test.why: UKHSA: boric acid containers should be filled to the marked line, and they should not be used for dipstick testing because the preservative affects the result.

whyNot.0: Boric acid affects dipstick results, so do not dipstick from this container.
whyNot.2: Diluting the specimen makes the culture unreliable.
whyNot.3: A loose lid risks leakage and contamination.

explain.body: Describe stool using the Bristol Stool Chart: types 1–2 suggest constipation, 3–4 are normal, 5–7 are increasingly loose. Record vomit amount, colour and contents and escalate anything abnormal.

test.q: On the Bristol Stool Chart, which types describe a normal stool?
options: Types 1 and 2
Types 5 and 6
Types 3 and 4
Types 6 and 7
test.why: Bladder and Bowel UK: a normal stool should be type 3 or 4.

whyNot.0: Types 1 and 2 are hard and lumpy, suggesting constipation.
whyNot.1: Types 5 and 6 are soft to mushy, moving towards diarrhoea.
whyNot.3: Types 6 and 7 are mushy to entirely liquid.
